result: SAP infusion resulted in extensive NA fiber loss in the VO, LO, and other cortical areas (A32, MO, M2, insula), with greater NA fiber volume in VO compared to LO in control animals.
evaluation: Claims C8, C9, and C36 are supported by statistical analyses (F-statistics with p<0.001) and histological data shown in Figures 1B-C and supplementary figures. The regional differences and extent of depletion are well-documented.

result: Initial instrumental learning and goal-directed behavior are intact following NA depletion in PFC regions, as demonstrated by normal acquisition of lever pressing and sensitivity to outcome devaluation.
evaluation: Claims C10-C12 are supported by statistical analyses showing no differences between control and SAP groups during initial training (F(1,53)=508.30, p<0.001 for training; F(1,53)=79.62, p<0.001 for devaluation effect) with no group differences or interactions.

result: NA depletion in the OFC impairs the ability to update action-outcome associations during reversal learning, with deficits present regardless of whether depletion occurred before or after initial training.
evaluation: Claims C13-C16 are supported by statistical analyses showing a significant devaluation × treatment interaction (F(1,53)=5.00, p<0.05) with control groups showing goal-directed behavior (F(1,53)=7.35, p<0.01) while depleted groups did not (F(1,53)=0.15, p=0.70). The effect was consistent across Pre and Post groups.

result: 6-OHDA infusion resulted in significant reduction of both TH-positive and NA fibers in the OFC and A32, with less off-site NA depletion compared to SAP, and no significant loss in the insula cortex.
evaluation: Claims C17, C18, C37, and C38 are supported by statistical analyses (F-statistics with p<0.001) and histological data shown in Figures 2B, 2D, and supplementary figures. The comparison between SAP and 6-OHDA depletion patterns is well-documented.

result: Combined DA and NA depletion (6-OHDA alone) impairs reversal learning and goal-directed behavior, while selective DA depletion (6-OHDA+Desi) leaves performance intact.
evaluation: Claims C19, C20, C22, and C34 are supported by statistical analyses showing that 6-OHDA rats responded more during training (F(1,18)=14.74, p<0.01) and failed to show goal-directed behavior in the test (F(1,18)=0.6, p=0.45), while 6-OHDA+Desi rats showed intact performance (F(1,15)=5.25, p<0.05 for devaluation effect).

result: Both 6-OHDA+Desi and control groups showed goal-directed behavior and biased their choice towards the action associated with the non-devalued outcome.
evaluation: Claim C21 is supported by statistical analysis showing a main effect of devaluation (F(1,15)=5.25, p<0.05) with no group effect (F(1,15)<0.001, p>0.975) or interaction (F(1,15)=0.17, p=0.69), indicating intact goal-directed behavior in both groups.

result: CAV2 vectors show retrograde transport to LC neurons with NA-specific expression of HA-tagged hM4Di and nonselective expression of mCherry at injection sites.
evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4B-D, demonstrating mCherry staining at injection sites and HA-immunoreactive cell bodies exclusively in the LC, consistent with the expected properties of the viral construct.

result: DCZ significantly decreased hM4Di/c-Fos colocalization following stress, validating the functional efficacy of the DREADDs construct.
evaluation: Claims C66 and C67 are supported by statistical analysis (t-test, p=0.034) showing ~35% decrease in hM4Di/c-Fos-positive cells with DCZ treatment, with stress inducing a fivefold increase in c-Fos expression in LC as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

result: Silencing LC:vlOFC NA projections impairs both encoding and recall of reversed action-outcome associations, as demonstrated by deficits when silencing occurs during training, testing, or both phases.
evaluation: Claims C28, C30, C35, and C47 are supported by statistical analyses showing a significant three-way interaction (F(1,23)=5.45, p<0.05) with only control rats (-/-) showing goal-directed behavior (F(1,23)=7.10, p<0.05), while all other conditions failed to show this preference.

result: Silencing LC:A32 NA projections does not impair goal-directed behavior based on initial or reversed instrumental contingencies.
evaluation: Claims C29 and C48 are supported by statistical analyses showing a main effect of devaluation (F(1,15)=5.76, p<0.05) with no effects of treatment during acquisition (F(1,15)=0.35, p=0.56) or test (F(1,15)=0.53, p=0.47), indicating intact goal-directed behavior.

result: NA inputs to the OFC are essential for updating goal-directed actions, with animals able to initially learn A-O contingencies but impaired when outcome identity is modified.
evaluation: Claims C31-C33 are supported by the convergent evidence from all three experimental approaches (SAP, 6-OHDA, and chemogenetic silencing) showing consistent deficits in reversal learning but intact initial learning following NA depletion or silencing.

result: NA fiber depletion in the OFC affects other PFC regions due to fibers of passage, though the OFC NA innervation is presumably specific with limited collateralization, and CAV2 vectors have limited spread from injection sites.
evaluation: Claims C23, C39-C42 are supported by experimental observations and citations to relevant literature (Chandler and Waterhouse, 2012; Plummer et al., 2020; Kebschull et al., 2016; Uematsu et al., 2017; Chandler et al., 2014; Cerpa et al., 2019; Schwarz et al., 2015) explaining the anatomical basis for off-target effects.

result: Different prefrontal regions have distinct roles in goal-directed behavior: A32 is needed for initial acquisition, insular cortex for outcome value recall, OFC for updating associations, and LC NA neurons track uncertainty and interact with PFC for behavioral flexibility.
evaluation: Claims C1-C7 are supported by extensive citations to prior literature establishing these functional roles. These claims provide the theoretical framework and prior knowledge context for the current study.

result: The current findings are consistent with previous work showing OFC involvement in updating action-outcome associations, though functional heterogeneity exists within OFC subregions.
evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by citations to relevant prior work (Parkes et al., 2018; Fresno et al., 2019; Bradfield and Hart, 2020; Izquierdo, 2017; Panayi and Killcross, 2018; Bradfield et al., 2018; Barreiros et al., 2021) that contextualizes the current findings.

result: NA inputs to different PFC regions have distinct functional roles: medial PFC NA is required for attentional regulation and set-shifting, while OFC NA affects cue-outcome reversal but not dimensional shifts.
evaluation: Claims C49-C54 are supported by citations to relevant literature (McGaughy et al., 2008; Newman et al., 2008; Cope et al., 2019; Mokler et al., 2017; Swanson et al., 2022) establishing the functional dissociation between NA inputs to different PFC regions.

result: DA signaling in A32 plays a role in contingency degradation detection via reward prediction error signals, while the role of OFC in contingency degradation remains unclear with mixed findings in the literature.
evaluation: Claims C55-C59 are supported by citations to relevant literature (Naneix et al., 2009; Montague et al., 2004; Schultz and Dickinson, 2000; Whyte et al., 2021; Zimmermann et al., 2017, 2018; Duan et al., 2021) discussing the role of DA and OFC in contingency degradation.

result: Reversal learning involves updating A-O contingencies without unlearning initial associations through state partitioning, with the OFC critically involved in this process and NA activity enabling behavioral flexibility when contingency changes are detected.
evaluation: Claims C60-C65 are supported by citations to relevant theoretical and empirical literature (Fresno et al., 2019; Parkes et al., 2018; Bradfield and Balleine, 2017; Hart and Balleine, 2016; McDannald et al., 2011; Wilson et al., 2014; Sadacca et al., 2017; Wikenheiser and Schoenbaum, 2016; Howard and Kahnt, 2021; Aston-Jones et al., 1997; Bouret and Sara, 2005) providing the theoretical framework for interpreting the results.

result: The LC displays anatomical and physiological variations between male and female rats, which is a limitation of the current study that used only male rats.
evaluation: Claim C46 is supported by citation to Joshi and Chandler, 2020 and represents an acknowledged limitation of the study that only examined male rats.

result: The study used 136 male Long-Evans rats aged 2-3 months, housed in pairs with ad libitum access to water and food, with ethical approval from the Bordeaux Ethics Committee.
evaluation: Claims C68-C70 are factual statements about the experimental subjects, housing conditions, and ethical approval that are standard methodological details.
